screens.title: Memory-Safe Architectures and Security
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll build a clear, practical picture of memory safety and the hardware tools that reduce risk. We start by naming the most common vulnerabilities — buffer overflow, use-after-free, dangling pointers, and integer overflows — and then explore how hardware changes the security trade-off. You will learn why some mechanisms, like ARM MTE, are practical for deployment while others, like CHERI, offer stronger guarantees at greater system cost. We'll use concrete examples: an allocator that reuses memory causing a use-after-free, a write past a buffer's end that overwrites nearby data, and the idea of a forged pointer versus an unforgeable capability. You will also see why performance and software compatibility steer which features reach production. By the end, you should be able to explain the basic operation of tagging, bounds checking, capabilities, and memory encryption, argue for their use in a particular system, and contrast security coverage with overhead and maturity. Consider: which combination of mechanisms would you choose for a mobile OS that must balance speed, compatibility, and attack resistance?

Memory-Safe Architectures and Security

Explore how hardware features such as bounds checking, memory tagging, and capabilities reduce common memory safety bugs while balancing performance and compatibility.

In this lesson
Definitions, hardware mechanisms, MTE and CHERI, and performance trade-offs.
Why it matters
Hardware can block exploit primitives before software sees malicious effects.
Overview
Memory safety failures let attackers corrupt control flow or read secrets. Hardware mechanisms provide layered defenses with different cost and coverage.
Vulnerability
Buffer overflow, use-after-free, dangling pointer
Hardware guard
Bounds checks, tags, capabilities, encryption, CFI
Trade-offs
Coverage vs. overhead vs. software changes
Visual concept
Three small cards represent MTE, CHERI, and Encryption with connecting thin lines implying progressive strength and cost. Each card lists one key property: tag width, capability fields, encryption scope.
Explore Key Topics
MTE
Low-overhead tagging to catch use-after-free and inter-object overflows.
CHERI
Capabilities with base, length, permissions, and unforgeable tag for full bounds enforcement.
Performance
Different mechanisms trade runtime overhead for coverage and required software changes.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these lessons you will be able to name and explain the core memory safety vulnerabilities and why they pose such a high risk. You will describe key hardware mechanisms — bounds checking, memory tagging, and capability-based addressing — and explain their core trade-offs of coverage, overhead, and maturity. You will also be able to outline ARM's Memory Tagging Extension and CHERI capability semantics: what each stores and what kinds of bugs they prevent. Finally, you'll learn to compare typical performance overheads and make a reasoned recommendation about which mechanism suits a given system. For example, you should be able to argue why MTE is attractive for an Android phone that must remain fast and compatible, and why CHERI might be chosen by a research OS that accepts more extensive software changes for stronger guarantees. These objectives prepare you to assess processors for memory-safety features and to design experiments to validate defenses.

screens.title: Memory safety vulnerabilities
screens.narratorSegment: Memory safety vulnerabilities arise when a program accesses memory in ways the language or system did not intend. A buffer overflow is a write beyond an allocated object that can overwrite adjacent data or code and enable control-flow hijacking. A use-after-free occurs when code continues to use a pointer after the allocator has returned that memory; that memory can be reallocated for another purpose and a later access will corrupt or leak data. A dangling pointer references deallocated memory and can appear identical to a live pointer, leading to subtle bugs. Integer overflow is often a root cause because a miscomputed length can allow a write past the buffer's end. For a concrete example, consider a network parser that reads an advertised length without checking bounds: an oversized length can cause a write beyond the buffer and overwrite a saved return address, enabling arbitrary execution. A common misconception is that these bugs always crash; often they corrupt memory silently and escalate to a security breach. The key takeaway is that memory-safety errors are both correctness and security problems: preventing them improves program reliability and reduces exploit surface. How would you detect whether an observed crash is an overflow or a use-after-free?

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 8.6 › Memory safety vulnerabilities
Definition
Common memory-safety bugs
  • Buffer overflow: write past an object's bounds that can corrupt adjacent state or control data.
  • Use-after-free: accessing memory after it was freed and possibly reallocated for another purpose.
  • Dangling pointer: a pointer that still references deallocated memory.
  • Integer overflow: arithmetic that yields an incorrect size causing incorrect allocations or copies.
Common mistake
Assuming a crash proves an exploit failed. Silent memory corruption is common and more dangerous.
Key takeaway
These bugs enable both data corruption and exploit primitives; preventing them reduces attack surface significantly.
Concrete example
A network parser trusts a length field and copies payload into a stack buffer. If the packet reports a larger length than the buffer, the write can overwrite the return address. An attacker crafts the length to place controlled values where a future return will use them. This is a classic buffer overflow exploitation path.
Check your understanding
  1. How could integer overflow in length computation enable an overflow?
  2. Why might a use-after-free not cause an immediate crash?
  3. What observable differences would you expect between a heap overflow and stack overflow?

screens.title: Hardware bounds checking and Intel MPX
screens.narratorSegment: Bounds checking in hardware attaches metadata to pointers so each memory access is verified against permitted ranges. Intel MPX added bounds registers to x86 so the processor could check each pointer dereference. In principle this reduces many buffer overflows, but MPX encountered practical issues: its runtime overhead grew large for some workloads, compilers and runtimes had to be adapted, and compatibility with existing binaries was limited. A typical misconception is that any hardware bounds check is automatically adoptable; in practice, integration effort and performance matter. For example, MPX required changes to code generation and libraries so bounds updates happened correctly; that complexity raised adoption friction. Contrast this with tag-based approaches like MTE, which are transparent to legacy pointers when not used. The concrete lesson is that architectural features must be both effective and usable: a mechanism that blocks bugs but imposes heavy overhead or complex toolchain changes may see little real-world use. Ask yourself: would you accept a 10–20% slowdown for full bounds checking in your server fleet, or prefer a lighter option with slightly weaker coverage? Hardware bounds checking and Intel MPX means even strong hardware checks fail to deploy if they impose high overhead or require disruptive toolchain changes.. In practical terms, why bounds registers were proposed and why mpx was deprecated. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 8.6 › Hardware bounds checking
Concept
Bounds checking and Intel MPX
Bounds checking stores metadata with pointers and verifies every access. MPX provided bounds registers and instructions on x86 to do this checking in hardware-assisted form.
Why MPX struggled
  • High overhead for some workloads (10–20%).
  • Needed compiler, runtime, and OS support.
  • Compatibility issues with legacy binaries.
Key takeaway
Strong protection is valuable only when it can be deployed with acceptable cost and effort.
Compare
MPX
High coverage for bounds checks but high overhead and integration cost; deprecated.
Tagging (MTE)
Lower overhead and easier integration; catches use-after-free and some cross-granularity overflows.
Reflection
When evaluating an architecture-level change, weigh not only theoretical coverage but the ecosystem work required to adopt it. If integration costs are high, even stronger mechanisms can fail in practice.

screens.title: ARM Memory Tagging Extension (MTE)
screens.narratorSegment: ARM's Memory Tagging Extension attaches a small tag to each 16-byte memory granule and stores a tag in the upper bits of pointers. On every memory access the hardware compares the pointer tag and the memory tag and raises a fault on mismatch. This design catches common errors like use-after-free when an allocator changes the memory tag at free and later reallocation uses a new tag. It also catches some buffer overflows when the overflow crosses a 16-byte boundary into a differently tagged granule. Crucially, MTE is not a complete solution: intra-object overflows within the same 16-byte granule can escape detection. The chapter reports low overhead for MTE, roughly one to two percent, which makes it attractive for deployment on mobile and server systems. A practical example is an allocator that assigns tag 3 to a block, frees it and then the kernel assigns tag 7 to the new occupant; an old pointer still bearing tag 3 causes a hardware fault when dereferenced. A common misconception is to expect MTE to stop every overflow; instead, treat it as a practical mitigation that dramatically reduces the most common exploit paths while keeping performance acceptable. How might you design tests that show both detected and undetected overflows under MTE?

keyIdea.text: MTE pairs small tags with memory granules to catch many use-after-free and inter-granule overflows with minimal cost, while accepting some remaining gaps.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 8.6 › ARM MTE
ARM Memory Tagging Extension — Process
MTE assigns tags to 16-byte memory granules and to pointer high bits and checks them on access.
Steps
  1. Allocator tags a memory granule with a 4-bit value when it is given to a program.
  2. Pointers carry a 4-bit tag in their high bits representing expected tag.
  3. On memory access hardware compares pointer tag and granule tag.
  4. Mismatches cause a fault, catching reuse or cross-granule overwrites.
Key takeaway
MTE is a pragmatic middle ground: wide deployment is possible because overhead is low, though it does not close every gap.
Concrete example
Allocate block A tagged 3. Free A. Allocate block B at same location but allocator assigns tag 7. An old pointer to A still carries tag 3; hardware raises a tag-mismatch fault when the old pointer is used, preventing unintended access.
Check your understanding
Design two short tests: one that triggers a tag mismatch and one intra-granule overflow that MTE would miss. Observing the fault in the first proves MTE is active; the second highlights its limits.

screens.title: MTE use-after-free demonstration (conceptual C)
screens.narratorSegment: This example shows how an MTE-capable system detects a use-after-free by changing the memory tag on free and reassigning a different tag on reallocation. The code is conceptual C: allocate memory, write a value, free it, reallocate a different object at the same location, and then access the old pointer. On MTE hardware the old pointer carries a stale tag and the load triggers a fault. This demonstrates the principle without requiring allocator internals: the allocator must change the tag when handing memory out. A common mistake is to assume any deallocation implies memory is overwritten; in many systems freed memory remains readable until reused. That window is where MTE adds value by making stale pointers fail fast. When testing, you would compile and run on a kernel and runtime that support MTE and check that the dereference raises the expected fault. The takeaway is that small experiments like this validate hardware behavior and expose both capabilities and edge cases of tagging. MTE use-after-free demonstration (conceptual C) means a concise test program can prove mte detects stale-pointer dereferences when the allocator changes tags on reuse.. In practical terms, a minimal allocate, free, reallocate, dereference sequence that mte would catch. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 8.6 › MTE Concept Demo
Conceptual C walkthrough
The following code is a conceptual sketch showing the allocate/free/reuse pattern that MTE detects when tags change on free and reallocation. It should be run on an MTE-enabled environment as an experiment rather than production code.
/* Conceptual C example (escape HTML) */
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
  char *p = malloc(32);           // allocate block A
  p[0] = 'x';                     // write via pointer with tag T1
  free(p);                        // allocator frees and may change memory tag

  char *q = malloc(32);           // new allocation at same address may get tag T2
  q[0] = 'y';                     // new occupant

  // dereference old pointer p: on MTE this should fault due to tag mismatch
  char c = p[0];
  printf("read: %c
", c);
  return 0;
}
Experiment steps
Run on MTE-enabled kernel. Observe a tag-mismatch fault when the stale pointer is accessed. This proves allocator-assigned tags are enforced by hardware.
Misconception
This test does not show all overflows are prevented; intra-granule overwrites within 16 bytes may not be detected.

screens.title: Capability-based addressing: CHERI and Morello
screens.narratorSegment: CHERI replaces raw pointers with capabilities: unforgeable tokens that carry a base address, a length, permissions (read, write, execute), and a validity tag. Because the tag is managed by hardware, software cannot fabricate valid capabilities by writing bits into memory. This prevents pointer forgery and enforces bounds on every dereference. A concrete example: instead of passing a raw pointer to a library routine, software hands a capability limited to the buffer range and write permission only when needed. An attempt by the library to access memory outside the capability's bounds is rejected by hardware. CHERI can therefore prevent buffer overflows, use-after-free, dangling pointer dereferences, and pointer forgery. The trade-off is significant: CHERI requires architectural and software changes, including extended ISA support and modified compilers and runtimes. Research platforms like Morello prototype these ideas. A common misconception is that capabilities are merely metadata; in CHERI they are hardware-enforced entities and cannot be made valid by user code. The key teaching point is that CHERI offers very high coverage but requires a broader ecosystem transition to realize its benefits. Capability-based addressing: CHERI and Morello means by making pointers unforgeable and embedding bounds and permissions, cheri prevents many memory-safety classes at the cost of architectural change.. In practical terms, how capabilities encode bounds, permissions, and unforgeability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 8.6 › CHERI Capabilities
CHERI capability structure
A capability includes base, length, permissions, and a hardware-validity tag that prevents forging.
Fields
  • Base and length: define permitted address range.
  • Permissions: read, write, execute controls tied to the capability.
  • Tag: a hardware bit indicating capability validity, preventing forgery.
Security guarantees
CHERI prevents all buffer overflows and use-after-free dereferences by bounding every pointer. It also stops pointer forgery because the validity tag cannot be set by software.
Morello
ARM research prototype that implements CHERI-like capabilities for exploration and evaluation.
Deployment note
CHERI gives strong guarantees but requires broad ISA and toolchain changes, keeping it in research and prototype stages for now.

screens.title: Memory encryption and control-flow integrity
screens.narratorSegment: Memory encryption and control-flow integrity tackle different threat models. Memory encryption like AMD's SME and SEV or Intel's TME encrypts R A M contents to defend against physical attacks such as cold boot or an adversary with physical access to DRAM. These designs protect confidentiality of memory but do not inherently prevent logical memory-safety bugs that arise within software. Control-flow integrity (CFI) focuses on preventing code-reuse attacks like return-oriented programming by ensuring that indirect branches and returns follow expected targets. Intel CET implements a shadow stack and indirect branch tracking to make ROP and JOP attacks much harder. These mechanisms are complementary: encryption secures against physical memory disclosure, while CFI stops certain exploit techniques used after memory corruption. A misconception is to treat one mechanism as a full solution; in practice, combining tagging or capabilities with CFI and encryption yields layered defense. For example, combining MTE to catch stale pointers with CET to protect return addresses reduces both the chances of corruption and the exploitability of any corruption that occurs. Memory encryption and control-flow integrity means encryption, tagging, capabilities, and cfi each address different vectors. combining them provides stronger, layered protection.. In practical terms, protecting physical memory and control-flow against low-level attacks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 9 › Chapter 8.6 › Encryption & CFI
Memory encryption and control-flow integrity
Encryption protects physical confidentiality; CFI protects control-flow integrity against code-reuse after corruption.
Memory encryption
AMD SME/SEV and Intel TME encrypt memory to prevent data disclosure from physical access. This is orthogonal to software memory-safety mechanisms.
Control-Flow Integrity
Intel CET and ARM BTI add shadow stacks and branch target validation to stop ROP/JOP even if memory is corrupted.
Example
Use MTE to detect stale pointers, and use CET to ensure return addresses cannot be redirected by an overflow. Encryption protects memory if an attacker obtains physical access.

screens.title: Performance and security coverage trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing a memory-safety mechanism requires balancing overhead, coverage, and maturity. Software sanitizers offer high coverage but incur large runtime slowdowns—often two to five times slower—making them unsuitable for production in many contexts. ARM MTE has very low overhead, around one to two percent, and delivers medium coverage: it catches use-after-free and some inter-granule overflows while remaining compatible with legacy code. Intel MPX aimed for strong bounds checks but suffered from high overhead and integration complexity, leading to deprecation. CHERI provides very high coverage—preventing buffer overflows, use-after-free, and pointer forgery—but imposes significant architectural and software changes and currently exists in research and prototype systems. Intel CET targets control-flow integrity with low overhead and medium coverage for control-flow-only attacks. When designing a system, list threat models and select a combination that addresses the highest-risk vectors while keeping acceptable cost. For instance, a production mobile OS could enable MTE and CET to get broad practical protection with minimal overhead, whereas a research OS might adopt CHERI to aim for near-complete memory safety at the expense of ecosystem changes. Performance and security coverage trade-offs means use low-overhead defenses where compatibility matters and stronger, disruptive mechanisms where full coverage justifies ecosystem change.. In practical terms, comparing sanitizers, mte, mpx, cheri, and cet. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: How to test for MTE and CET on real hardware
screens.narratorSegment: To validate memory-safety features on your processor start by checking C P U feature flags. On ARM look for the 'mte' flag and on Intel look for 'cet' in the C P U feature listing. If MTE is present, design a small test: allocate memory, tag it, free it, reallocate with a different tag, then attempt an access through the stale pointer and verify the kernel reports a tag-mismatch fault. If CET is present, construct a controlled call/return sequence and check that return address corruption does not redirect control flow because of a shadow stack or indirect branch checking. A common pitfall is running these tests without proper kernel and runtime support; feature flags alone are not enough. When you cannot run the hardware test, write a short lab report describing the expected sequence: allocate, set tag, free, reallocate, and attempt stale access. The chapter suggests this as a concrete hands-on task to prove both the presence of a feature and its practical behavior. End by reflecting on how the observed behavior maps to the coverage and overhead trade-offs you studied earlier.

Module 9 › Chapter 8.6 › Hands-on Activity
Testing steps
  1. Check CPU feature flags for 'mte' or 'cet' to detect advertised support.
  2. If MTE is present, write an allocate/free/reallocate test that triggers a tag mismatch on stale access.
  3. If CET is present, test shadow-stack enforcement by attempting to redirect return addresses in a controlled program.
  4. Run tests under a kernel and runtime that enable the feature; log faults and verify behavior.
Example report
Describe the sequence, the observed fault type, and whether the behavior matched expectations. If you cannot run the test, describe the expected kernel fault and why it would occur.
Caution
Do not assume feature flags guarantee full protection. Kernel support and allocator behavior determine effectiveness.

screens.title: Why Intel deprecated MPX while ARM deployed MTE
screens.narratorSegment: Intel deprecated MPX because despite decent theoretical coverage, real-world adoption stalled. MPX demanded compiler, runtime, and OS changes, and in many workloads it added significant overhead, sometimes in the 10–20% range. Those two difficulties—performance and integration complexity—created a high adoption barrier. In contrast, ARM's MTE hits a different point in the design space: it offers lower overhead, approximately one to two percent, and can be integrated by allocators and runtimes without invalidating legacy binaries that don't opt in. MTE mainly detects use-after-free and cross-granule overflows, which addresses a large portion of exploit techniques in practice. The chapter's assessment is that practical security wins when mechanisms fit existing ecosystems and keep cost low. A common misunderstanding is to compare only theoretical coverage; instead, successful deployment depends on how easily software stacks can adopt the mechanism and whether performance remains acceptable. When recommending a feature for production, always weigh ecosystem friction and measured overhead along with coverage. Why Intel deprecated MPX while ARM deployed MTE means mpx's strong bounds checking failed in practice due to overhead and integration costs; mte succeeded by balancing protection and compatibility.. In practical terms, a concrete comparison of integration, overhead, and compatibility. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll build a clear, practical picture of memory safety and the hardware tools that reduce risk. We start by naming the most common vulnerabilities — buffer overflow, use-after-free, dangling pointers, and integer overflows — and then explore how hardware changes the security trade-off. You will learn why some mechanisms, like ARM MTE, are practical for deployment while others, like CHERI, offer stronger guarantees at greater system cost. We'll use concrete examples: an allocator that reuses memory causing a use-after-free, a write past a buffer's end that overwrites nearby data, and the idea of a forged pointer versus an unforgeable capability. You will also see why performance and software compatibility steer which features reach production. By the end, you should be able to explain the basic operation of tagging, bounds checking, capabilities, and memory encryption, argue for their use in a particular system, and contrast security coverage with overhead and maturity. Consider: which combination of mechanisms would you choose for a mobile OS that must balance speed, compatibility, and attack resistance?

By the end of these lessons you will be able to name and explain the core memory safety vulnerabilities and why they pose such a high risk. You will describe key hardware mechanisms — bounds checking, memory tagging, and capability-based addressing — and explain their core trade-offs of coverage, overhead, and maturity. You will also be able to outline ARM's Memory Tagging Extension and CHERI capability semantics: what each stores and what kinds of bugs they prevent. Finally, you'll learn to compare typical performance overheads and make a reasoned recommendation about which mechanism suits a given system. For example, you should be able to argue why MTE is attractive for an Android phone that must remain fast and compatible, and why CHERI might be chosen by a research OS that accepts more extensive software changes for stronger guarantees. These objectives prepare you to assess processors for memory-safety features and to design experiments to validate defenses.

This second objectives slide focuses on applied skills. You should be able to check C P U feature flags and interpret what they mean for a platform's security posture. For ARM-based systems you will learn to recognize the presence of MTE and understand a simple experiment: allocate memory, tag it, free it, reallocate with a different tag, and then attempt to access the old pointer to see if hardware raises a fault. You will also be able to summarize how CHERI capabilities would stop a buffer overflow by enforcing bounds on every pointer. Finally, you should be ready to write a brief assessment recommending which memory-safety mechanisms to enable for a given use case, weighing deployment maturity and runtime cost. These applied objectives prepare you to move from theory to measurement and to craft defensible recommendations for system configuration or design.

Memory safety vulnerabilities arise when a program accesses memory in ways the language or system did not intend. A buffer overflow is a write beyond an allocated object that can overwrite adjacent data or code and enable control-flow hijacking. A use-after-free occurs when code continues to use a pointer after the allocator has returned that memory; that memory can be reallocated for another purpose and a later access will corrupt or leak data. A dangling pointer references deallocated memory and can appear identical to a live pointer, leading to subtle bugs. Integer overflow is often a root cause because a miscomputed length can allow a write past the buffer's end. For a concrete example, consider a network parser that reads an advertised length without checking bounds: an oversized length can cause a write beyond the buffer and overwrite a saved return address, enabling arbitrary execution. A common misconception is that these bugs always crash; often they corrupt memory silently and escalate to a security breach. The key takeaway is that memory-safety errors are both correctness and security problems: preventing them improves program reliability and reduces exploit surface. How would you detect whether an observed crash is an overflow or a use-after-free?

Bounds checking in hardware attaches metadata to pointers so each memory access is verified against permitted ranges. Intel MPX added bounds registers to x86 so the processor could check each pointer dereference. In principle this reduces many buffer overflows, but MPX encountered practical issues: its runtime overhead grew large for some workloads, compilers and runtimes had to be adapted, and compatibility with existing binaries was limited. A typical misconception is that any hardware bounds check is automatically adoptable; in practice, integration effort and performance matter. For example, MPX required changes to code generation and libraries so bounds updates happened correctly; that complexity raised adoption friction. Contrast this with tag-based approaches like MTE, which are transparent to legacy pointers when not used. The concrete lesson is that architectural features must be both effective and usable: a mechanism that blocks bugs but imposes heavy overhead or complex toolchain changes may see little real-world use. Ask yourself: would you accept a 10–20% slowdown for full bounds checking in your server fleet, or prefer a lighter option with slightly weaker coverage? Hardware bounds checking and Intel MPX means even strong hardware checks fail to deploy if they impose high overhead or require disruptive toolchain changes.. In practical terms, why bounds registers were proposed and why mpx was deprecated. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

ARM's Memory Tagging Extension attaches a small tag to each 16-byte memory granule and stores a tag in the upper bits of pointers. On every memory access the hardware compares the pointer tag and the memory tag and raises a fault on mismatch. This design catches common errors like use-after-free when an allocator changes the memory tag at free and later reallocation uses a new tag. It also catches some buffer overflows when the overflow crosses a 16-byte boundary into a differently tagged granule. Crucially, MTE is not a complete solution: intra-object overflows within the same 16-byte granule can escape detection. The chapter reports low overhead for MTE, roughly one to two percent, which makes it attractive for deployment on mobile and server systems. A practical example is an allocator that assigns tag 3 to a block, frees it and then the kernel assigns tag 7 to the new occupant; an old pointer still bearing tag 3 causes a hardware fault when dereferenced. A common misconception is to expect MTE to stop every overflow; instead, treat it as a practical mitigation that dramatically reduces the most common exploit paths while keeping performance acceptable. How might you design tests that show both detected and undetected overflows under MTE?

This example shows how an MTE-capable system detects a use-after-free by changing the memory tag on free and reassigning a different tag on reallocation. The code is conceptual C: allocate memory, write a value, free it, reallocate a different object at the same location, and then access the old pointer. On MTE hardware the old pointer carries a stale tag and the load triggers a fault. This demonstrates the principle without requiring allocator internals: the allocator must change the tag when handing memory out. A common mistake is to assume any deallocation implies memory is overwritten; in many systems freed memory remains readable until reused. That window is where MTE adds value by making stale pointers fail fast. When testing, you would compile and run on a kernel and runtime that support MTE and check that the dereference raises the expected fault. The takeaway is that small experiments like this validate hardware behavior and expose both capabilities and edge cases of tagging. MTE use-after-free demonstration (conceptual C) means a concise test program can prove mte detects stale-pointer dereferences when the allocator changes tags on reuse.. In practical terms, a minimal allocate, free, reallocate, dereference sequence that mte would catch. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

CHERI replaces raw pointers with capabilities: unforgeable tokens that carry a base address, a length, permissions (read, write, execute), and a validity tag. Because the tag is managed by hardware, software cannot fabricate valid capabilities by writing bits into memory. This prevents pointer forgery and enforces bounds on every dereference. A concrete example: instead of passing a raw pointer to a library routine, software hands a capability limited to the buffer range and write permission only when needed. An attempt by the library to access memory outside the capability's bounds is rejected by hardware. CHERI can therefore prevent buffer overflows, use-after-free, dangling pointer dereferences, and pointer forgery. The trade-off is significant: CHERI requires architectural and software changes, including extended ISA support and modified compilers and runtimes. Research platforms like Morello prototype these ideas. A common misconception is that capabilities are merely metadata; in CHERI they are hardware-enforced entities and cannot be made valid by user code. The key teaching point is that CHERI offers very high coverage but requires a broader ecosystem transition to realize its benefits. In practical terms, how capabilities encode bounds, permissions, and unforgeability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Memory encryption and control-flow integrity tackle different threat models.
